title: A Non-Simple View of Ambiguity
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood uses the problem of ambiguity to challenge the Simple View of Reading, the formula that decoding plus comprehension equals reading. He argues that readers constantly manage ambiguity in real texts, so sentence comprehension and world knowledge cannot be separated from decoding. Examples include a sentence about a boy with tears in his coat and a politician's carefully ambiguous use of the word know. He questions why Gough and colleagues tinkered with the formula over time and why complexity was divided into two equal parts, and points to recent literacy scholars who concede reading is complex. The argument is a skeptical, rhetorical challenge to oversimplified reading models and the teaching they inspire. Some quoted passages are missing from the text as archived.
points: Ambiguity shows that decoding and comprehension are complementary rather than separable components of reading.
Phonics knowledge alone cannot resolve a sentence like the boy with tears in his coat; sentence comprehension and world knowledge are required.
Mature readers must manage ambiguity charitably as part of co-creating meaning with the writer.
The author questions whether a two-part formula for reading, and by extension for teaching, can capture real classroom complexity.
The Simple View's own authors acknowledged that reading is complex, so simplified uses of it overstate the model.
quotes: Such writers harbor a righteous fear of hidden ambiguity on important points in their public discourse because it can damage not only their immediate message, but also the confidence their readership might have in their past and future writing. A key challenge in this genre is to minimize the threat.

Ambiguity can be treacherous for readers in search of evidence and fact even with a trusted writer. Every text carries some ambiguity; readers are responsible for managing it charitably as part of the agreement to co-create meaning.

Phonics ain’t going to help you here. You need sentence comprehension. This example complicates any simple view by illustrating just one obvious way that decoding and comprehension are not separate, but complementary.

The silent K means nothing without sentence comprehension and world knowledge. You try your best, you “know” that he “knew,” but your knowledge is not to be found in his words even if they were phonetically regular. Orthography and lexical knowledge are insufficient; semantic knowledge brings you closer to his intention.
It’s so simple, eh? Decoding plus Comprehension equals reading? This is real life we are discussing—real children, real teachers, real citizens, real scientists.

How do we square a responsible reading of “I didn’t even know him” with the “simple view of reading”? What does decoding mean when a sentence has been double coded to double cross? What happens to mature readers when their early induction years into reading were informed by a simple view of the simple view of reading?
